Regarding how processors work and all that, that is indeed a particular problem because they are possibly too complex for a human to fully understand, as a modern CPU has billions of transistors. (Or millions, maybe.) CPU's have layers upon layers of complexity, most of which is hidden from us, and at the code level we can probably best understand how a processor works by its instruction set, which determines how machine code and ASM for that CPU will look like. With early processors, ASM and machine code were pretty close to what the CPU was physically doing, but as things got complicated, machine code represents something more abstract. Writing programs in C/C++ will give you a general idea of what ASM is like; a compiler just takes your C code and converts it automatically into ASM. If you wanted to get more familiar with what a processor does or can do, writing ASM for an old/simple processor is a good exercise, and that code could be run on an emulator or maybe linked for a modern CPU. When I was in college, our ASM class was about how to program the 8080 processor, a CPU made by Intel in 1974.

Opening up a computer and physically looking at it is also fun. You can learn to identify the main parts of the computer and what's on the motherboard.

ASM is common for assembly language, which is a way of writing computer programs that is very, very close to machine code. It's virtually one step away from machine code because basically the numeric codes are replaced with words you can remember, like "MOVE" and stuff like that. An assembler will "link" that code into pure numbers so it'll run on the hardware, but whatever you write in ASM is directly talking to the CPU, and it just won't work on another kind of CPU that isn't compatible. A compiler is another kind of program that takes higher level code like C code and convert it into ASM that could run on your particular processor. A large amount of computer code that gets written goes through this process, where a human writes it in some abstract language, and then it goes through the automated process of being compiled and linked. Sometimes something else is done, like in the case of Python which is run by an interpreter. An interpreter will read your instructions and carry them out right away without compiling and linking; this can make writing and running code a lot easier, but it runs slower because the interpreter is just another layer that gets in the way.

One reason someone might write ASM code is that they need to optimize the code to execute as fast as physically possible, which couldn't take place with a compiler that churns out more generic codes. It's often considered a waste of time now, though. In some cases a compiled program can run just as fast, nearly as fast, or nobody cares if it's not as fast. :)
